title: Trending Hashtags
prompt: Design the 'Trending now' feature of a social platform: show the top 100 hashtags over the last 5 minutes, hour and day, globally and per country, refreshed every few seconds.

clarify.q: Do we want the most used tags, or the ones rising fastest?
clarify.why: Most-used gives the same evergreen tags every day. Trending means growth against a baseline, which needs counts for older windows too, not just the current one.

clarify.q: How exact must the counts and the order be?
clarify.why: If being off by ~1% and occasionally swapping #99 and #101 is fine, a fixed-size sketch replaces an unbounded exact map. If shown counts must be exact, we track exact counts for a small candidate set.

clarify.q: Which windows and which slices (global, country, language)?
clarify.why: Every window × slice combination is its own top-K. 3 windows × 201 slices is 603 lists, and memory scales with that product.

clarify.q: How fresh: real-time, every few seconds, or every minute?
clarify.why: Few seconds needs a streaming pipeline with in-memory state. Every 10 minutes could be a micro-batch job over the log.

clarify.q: Does one account posting a tag 10 000 times count 10 000 times?
clarify.why: Counting events lets bots game trends. Counting distinct users per tag needs a cardinality sketch per candidate.

clarify.q: What events count: posts only, or also likes and shares of posts with the tag?
clarify.why: Including engagement raises the event rate roughly 20×. That changes ingest sizing but not the counting design.

functional: Return the top 100 trending hashtags for windows 5 min, 1 h and 24 h.
Support a global list and one list per country (200 countries).
Each entry shows the hashtag, an approximate count, and its rank change since the last refresh.
Lists refresh at least every 10 s.
Blocked or unsafe hashtags never appear, even if they are trending.
nonFunctional: Read API p99 under 50 ms; lists are served from cache.
Counts within ~1% of truth for anything in the top 100; ranking errors only between items with near-equal counts.
Memory bounded regardless of how many distinct hashtags appear, including spam floods of random tags.
Losing a worker may blur one refresh but must not empty the list.
outOfScope: Long-term analytics such as 'top tags of the year'.
The moderation model; we consume its blocklist.

assumptions: 10 B hashtag events per day (a post or engagement carrying a tag); peak 3× average
~50 M distinct hashtags per day, ~8 M per hour, ~2 M per 5 minutes; most appear once
Exact hash-map entry ≈ 60 bytes (tag string, count, map overhead)
Count-min sketch: depth 5 rows of 4-byte counters

steps.label: Ingest bandwidth
steps.result: Small: the log is not the bottleneck

steps.label: Exact counting, global 1 h window
steps.math: 12 five-minute maps × 2 M keys × 60 B ≈ 1.4 GB
steps.result: ≈ 1.4 GB, and it grows with every random tag a bot invents

steps.label: Sketch for the 1 h window
steps.result: 21 MB fixed; any count over-estimated by at most ~1 080 in 99.3% of lookups

steps.label: Sketch for the 24 h window
steps.result: 84 MB; ~6 500 error vs top-100 daily tags in the hundreds of thousands

steps.label: Per-country sketches
steps.math: width 2^16, depth 4: 4 × 65 536 × 4 B = 1 MB; × 200 countries × 12 buckets
steps.result: ≈ 2.4 GB for the 1 h ring across all countries

estimates.takeaway:
Throughput is easy: ~350 k small events/s at peak. The design is decided by memory per window and slice, and by the long tail. Exact maps cost memory per distinct tag, and most tags appear once, so most of that memory is spent on noise. A spam bot inventing random tags can grow them without limit.

A count-min sketch costs fixed memory per window. Its error is tied to the window's total volume (~1 080 on 417 M events), which is small next to the counts of anything that is genuinely trending. So we use sketches to find candidates, and keep exact counters only for a few thousand tags per list.

api.returns: 200 { asOf, items: [{ tag, count, approx: true, rank, rankDelta }] }
api.note: Served from a cache key per (window, country). asOf tells the client how fresh the list is.

api.body: { tag, userId, country, lang, eventTime, kind: post|like|share }
api.note: Tags are normalized (lowercase, Unicode NFKC) at the producer so #Café and #cafe count as one.

api.returns: written to the cache by the ranker
api.note: Snapshot every 10 s; the read path never computes anything.
Adds to a blocklist that the ranker filters on every snapshot.

entities.name: Window sketch
entities.store: In memory on aggregator workers, checkpointed every minute
fields: identical on every worker so sketches can be added
entities.why: Fixed-size counts for every tag in a time bucket. A sliding window is the sum of the buckets inside it.

entities.name: Candidate heap
entities.store: In memory, per window and slice
entities.why: The sketch cannot list its keys, so we keep the top ~1 000 candidates by estimate, with exact counts and distinct users only for them.

entities.name: Trending snapshot
entities.why: What the API serves. Tiny (~10 KB), replaced every 10 s, replicated to every region.

entities.name: Baseline
entities.store: Column store, hourly counts for the top ~100 k tags
entities.why: Lets the ranker tell 'always big' from 'suddenly big'. Updated by an hourly batch job.

data.note:
Nothing here is a source of truth except the event log. Every structure is rebuildable by replaying the last 24 h of events, so losing state costs freshness, not correctness.

The sketches use the same width, depth and hash seeds on every worker. That makes merging two sketches a plain element-wise addition, and the merged sketch has exactly the same error guarantee as one built from all events.

hld.summary:
Post and engagement services emit hashtag.used events to a log topic, partitioned by userId. That spreads load evenly even when one tag is exploding. Stage-1 workers (32 of them) each keep, per 5-minute bucket and per slice, a count-min sketch plus a local candidate heap of ~1 000 tags. Every 10 s they ship their delta sketches and candidate lists to the stage-2 merger.

The merger adds the sketches into a ring of bucket sketches per window, unions the candidate lists, and re-estimates every candidate against the merged window sketch. A ranker then scores candidates against their baseline, drops blocked tags and tags driven by very few users, and writes a top-100 snapshot per (window, country) to Redis. The read API only reads Redis.

diagram.title: Two-stage counting pipeline
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  PS[Post and engagement services] --> LOG["hashtag.used topic"]
  LOG --> W1["Stage 1 worker 1: sketch and heap"]
  LOG --> W2["Stage 1 worker 2: sketch and heap"]
  LOG --> WN["Stage 1 worker 32: sketch and heap"]
  W1 --> M["Stage 2 merger: window rings"]
  W2 --> M
  WN --> M
  M --> RK[Ranker]
  BL[(Baseline store)] --> RK
  BK[Blocklist] --> RK
  RK --> RC[(Redis snapshots)]
  RC --> API[Trending API]
  API --> APP[Clients]

flows.title: Counting one event
steps: Worker reads hashtag.used for #finalgoal from country BR.
It increments the global and BR sketches for the current 5-minute bucket: 5 hashed counters each.
It estimates #finalgoal's count from the sketch; if it beats the smallest entry in the local heap, it inserts or updates it.
It adds the userId to the tag's HyperLogLog if the tag is a candidate.

flows.title: Refreshing the lists (every 10 s)
steps: Each worker sends its sketch deltas since the last flush and its candidate lists to the merger.
Merger adds deltas into the current bucket of each window ring and updates the running window sums.
It unions candidates from all workers and re-estimates each against the merged window sketch.
Ranker computes a trend score versus baseline, filters blocked tags and low distinct-user tags, and keeps the top 100.
Snapshot is written to Redis with asOf; the API serves it until the next one.

flows.title: Window slides
steps: When a new 5-minute bucket starts, the merger subtracts the bucket that just left the 1 h window from the running 1 h sketch.
Sketch counters only ever had that bucket's counts added, so subtracting them is exact and cannot go negative.
Candidate estimates drop accordingly; tags falling below the heap threshold are evicted.

deepDives.title: Exact counts or a count-min sketch plus a heap
deepDives.problem: To rank hashtags we need a count per tag per window. Exact counting needs one entry for every distinct tag, and most tags are typos or one-offs, so the memory goes to tags that will never trend. A spam bot can push it up without limit. A sketch has fixed memory but over-counts, and it cannot list which tags it has seen.

options.name: Exact hash map per bucket
options.how: Map tag to count for each 5-minute bucket; sum buckets for a window; sort or heap-select the top 100.
pros: Exact counts, no explaining error bars
Simple to test
cons: ≈ 1.4 GB per global 1 h window at our numbers, more per slice
Memory grows with every new tag, so random-tag spam is a memory attack
Merging across workers means shuffling every distinct key

options.name: Count-min sketch plus a top-K heap
options.how: A d × w grid of counters. Each event increments one counter per row, chosen by that row's hash. A tag's estimate is the minimum of its d counters. A heap keeps the ~1 000 tags with the highest estimates seen so far.
pros: Fixed memory: 21 MB for the 1 h global window
Never under-counts; over-count is bounded
Sketches merge by addition
cons: Over-counts low-volume tags much more in relative terms
Cannot enumerate keys; the heap must catch candidates as they stream past
A tag can be over-estimated into the heap by collisions

options.name: Space-saving style counters
options.how: Keep exactly M counters; when a new tag arrives and all are taken, replace the smallest and inherit its count as error.
pros: Lists the heavy hitters directly
Tight error for skewed data
cons: Harder to merge across workers and to slide over time
Error per item must be tracked to reason about guarantees

deepDives.choice:
Count-min sketch plus a heap, with exact tracking for candidates. The guarantee in plain words: with width w, each estimate is at most the true count plus (2.72 / w) × N, where N is the total events in the window. That holds for all but e-d of lookups; with d = 5, that is 1 in ~150.

At 417 M events per hour and w = 220, the over-count is at most ~1 080. A top-100 hourly tag has tens of thousands of uses, so the error is a few percent at worst and usually far less, because real data is skewed. Using conservative update (only raise the counters that are at the current minimum) reduces over-counting further in practice.

Once a tag enters the heap we also count it exactly, so the number we display is real from that point on. If product required exact counts for all tags, I would switch to exact maps with a minimum-count filter, and pay for the shuffle.

deepDives.title: Sliding windows
deepDives.problem: 'Last hour' moves every second. Recounting from raw events on every refresh is wasteful, and a sketch cannot forget individual old events once they are added.

options.name: Ring of bucket sketches
options.how: One sketch per 5-minute bucket. Keep a running window sum: add events to the current bucket and the sum; when a bucket expires, subtract it from the sum and drop it.
pros: Exact window semantics at bucket granularity
Subtraction is exact because the expired bucket is exactly what was added
Refresh cost is constant
cons: The window edge jumps in 5-minute steps
Memory = buckets × sketch size (12 × 21 MB for the global hour)

options.name: Exponential decay
options.how: Multiply all counts by a decay factor over time so old events fade instead of expiring.
pros: One sketch per window, smooth ranking
Naturally favours recent activity, which matches 'trending'
cons: No clean 'last hour' meaning for the displayed number
Decaying a 5 M-counter sketch must be done lazily (scale a global factor) to be cheap

options.name: Recompute per refresh from a micro-batch
options.how: Every minute, a batch job counts the last hour from the log.
pros: Simple and exact
cons: Rereads 417 M events every minute
Freshness bounded by the job runtime

deepDives.choice:
A ring of bucket sketches: 12 five-minute buckets for the 1 h window, and 24 one-hour buckets with a wider sketch for 24 h. The 5-minute window is just the current bucket plus the previous one, weighted by overlap. A 5-minute jump on a 1 h window is invisible to users, and the displayed count keeps a clear meaning.

For the ranking score itself, a smooth decay is nice. The ranker can weight recent buckets more without changing storage. If memory became tight with many more slices, I would move long windows to exponential decay and keep rings only for the short ones.

deepDives.title: Merging partial top-K across workers
deepDives.problem: The work is split across 32 workers. If each sends only its local top list, can we compute the global top 100 from them? Only sometimes. A tag can rank 150th on every worker and still be first overall once the counts are added up.

options.name: Partition events by hashtag
options.how: Each tag lives on exactly one worker, so the union of per-worker top-100 lists contains the true global top 100.
pros: Merge is exact: each tag's full count is in one place
Simple to reason about
cons: A viral tag sends 50 k events/s to one worker, the hot-key problem
Every slice needs the same key routing, and repartitioning moves state

options.name: Partition by user, merge top lists only
options.how: Each worker returns its local top 100; the merger sums counts per tag across the lists.
pros: Even load whatever the tag skew
Tiny merge payload
cons: Not correct: a tag missing from some workers' lists is under-counted or missed entirely
Error is silent

options.name: Partition by user, merge sketches plus wider candidate lists
options.how: Workers send sketch deltas and their top ~1 000 candidates. Merger adds sketches (exact merge), unions candidates, and re-estimates each from the merged sketch.
pros: Even load
Each candidate gets a full-volume estimate, not a partial one
A simple check tells us when a miss was possible
cons: Ships sketch deltas: sent sparse, each 10 s flush is ~36 k events × 5 counters × 8 B ≈ 1.5 MB per worker, ≈ 5 MB/s for 32 workers on the global sketch alone
Still possible to miss a tag absent from every candidate list

deepDives.choice:
Partition by user and merge sketches plus wide candidate lists. Why it is not exact: a tag only gets considered if at least one worker had it in its top 1 000. The check is easy. Let ti be the 1 000th count on worker i. A tag on no list has a global count of at most the sum of all ti. If that sum is below the 100th count in our result, nothing was missed.

With random partitioning each worker sees ~1/32 of every tag, so the sum is about the global 1 000th count, far below the 100th. The merger logs whenever the check fails and widens the candidate lists. If one region's traffic were tiny and flat, I would partition by tag there with local pre-aggregation instead.

diagram.title: Why local top lists are not enough
diagram.src:
flowchart TD
  A["Worker 1 top 3: x 900, y 850, z 800"] --> M[Naive merge]
  B["Worker 2 top 3: p 910, q 860, r 820"] --> M
  C["Tag t: 790 on each worker, rank 4 on both"] -.-> M
  M --> R["Merged top 3: p 910, x 900, q 860"]
  R --> T["True leader is t with 1580, but it was never sent"]

deepDives.title: From 'most used' to 'trending' and harder to game
deepDives.problem: The raw top 100 is mostly the same evergreen tags every hour (#love, #photo). People expect 'what is happening now'. Raw counts are also easy to game: one bot farm posting a tag 100 k times can top the list.

options.name: Raw count
pros: Easy to explain
cons: Evergreen tags dominate
Trivially gamed by volume

options.name: Growth against a baseline
options.how: Score = (current − expected) / sqrt(expected + c), where expected comes from the same hour of week averaged over 4 weeks, or the previous window.
pros: New events rise fast; evergreen tags sit near zero
The square root damps noise from tiny tags
cons: Needs baselines for candidates, which means an extra store
Brand-new tags have no baseline, so c must be tuned

options.name: Count distinct users, not events
options.how: Keep a HyperLogLog of userIds per candidate; use distinct users in the score and require a minimum (e.g. 200).
pros: One account cannot move the list
HLL is ~1.5 KB per candidate with ~2% error
cons: Only affordable for candidates, not every tag
Coordinated bot farms with many accounts still need a fraud signal

deepDives.choice: Score by growth against baseline, computed on distinct users, with a minimum distinct-user floor and the blocklist applied last. The sketch finds candidates by volume; the ranker decides what is trending. Keeping those two jobs separate lets product tune the score without touching the counting pipeline. If trend manipulation became a real problem, I would weight users by account age and trust score from the integrity team.

failures: Its partitions move to another worker, which restores the last 1-minute checkpoint and replays the log from there; one refresh may undercount slightly.
A standby merger restores the window rings from checkpoint and replays the last minute of deltas; meanwhile the API keeps serving the last snapshot with an older asOf.
Spam flood of millions of random tags
Sketch memory is unchanged; random tags never reach the heap. Distinct-user floors stop a single account from trending a tag.
A blocked or harmful tag starts trending
Ranker filters against the blocklist on every snapshot, so a block takes effect within 10 s.
Redis node holding snapshots is lost
Snapshots are tiny and rewritten every 10 s; replica failover, or the next snapshot repopulates within seconds.
Event spike at a global event (5× normal)
Log absorbs the burst; workers scale out by partition; sketch error grows with N but stays small relative to the tags that are spiking.
scale: 10× events: add partitions and stage-1 workers. Sketch sizes do not change, but error grows with N, so widen the 24 h sketch from 2^22 to 2^24 (~335 MB) to keep the same relative error.
More slices (city, language): size each sketch to its slice's volume, as country sketches already are, and only build slices with enough traffic to trend.
Multi-region: run stage 1 in each region and ship sketch deltas to one global merger. Sketches add across regions as they do across workers, and the global list is a few seconds staler.

followups.q: Explain the count-min sketch error to a product manager.
answer: Every count we show might be a little high, never low.
How much too high is limited by the total traffic in the window divided by the sketch width: about 1 000 extra uses on an hour of 417 M events.
Trending tags have tens of thousands of uses, so the order of the top items is reliable; only near-ties can swap.

followups.q: Why not just use a sorted set in Redis with ZINCRBY?
answer: At 350 k increments/s a single sorted set is one hot key on one shard.
The set grows with every distinct tag, the same unbounded-memory problem.
Sliding windows would need one set per bucket and expensive ZUNIONSTOREs; fine for a prototype at 1 k events/s.

followups.q: How would you show exact counts if legal or product insisted?
answer: Keep the sketch only to choose candidates.
Run an exact count for the final top 100 from a batch over the log, a few minutes behind.
Display exact counts with a slightly older asOf; ranking stays live.

followups.q: How do you test that the sketch is accurate enough?
answer: Replay a day of real events into both the sketch pipeline and an exact batch count.
Measure overlap of top 100 and the maximum relative count error.
Alert in production on a sampled exact recount of the top 100 every hour.

followups.q: What changes for songs instead of hashtags?
answer: Key space is a fixed catalogue (~100 M songs) with numeric IDs, so exact counts become more attractive.
Plays may need a minimum listen time before counting.
Baselines matter even more: big catalogue artists dominate raw counts.

mistakes: Using one Redis sorted set for everything and not noticing the hot key or the unbounded memory.
Merging per-worker top-K lists and claiming the result is exact.
Describing a count-min sketch without saying what its error depends on (width and total volume) or that it only over-counts.
Treating 'most frequent' and 'trending' as the same thing.
Recomputing the whole window from raw events on every refresh.

Stated the sketch error bound in plain words with a worked number
Explained why sketches merge by addition and require identical hash seeds
Handled window expiry by subtracting expired bucket sketches
Chose a partitioning scheme and addressed hot tags
staff: Explained why merging partial top-K lists can miss the true leader and gave a check for when it cannot
Separated candidate finding (sketch) from ranking (baseline growth, distinct users, blocklist)
Designed for adversarial inputs: random-tag floods and single-account spam
Described how to validate approximation quality against an exact batch count
